title: Test day five
hookLine: notice what you love: a boy steals pears he doesn't want, and Augustine learns what really moves a person
tomorrow: what was the world still missing on the seventh day?

cards: Some songs you skip after a few seconds. One song you play again before it's even over, and nobody has to make you. Now a night in North Africa, long ago.
Late one night, a teenage boy and his friends shake down a pear tree near his family's vineyard. The pears aren't even good. They take a few bites and throw the rest to the pigs.
Years later, that boy, Augustine, still can't stop asking why he did it.

teach.h: A PEAR TREE, AND A QUESTION.
teach.b: He tells the story in his Confessions, a long book spoken to God. His answer surprises him. He didn't love the pears.

teach.h: HE LOVED THE STEALING, AND THE FRIENDS.
teach.b: He loved the stealing, and the friends he did it with; alone, he says, he would never have done it. His answer grows into a teaching that runs through the whole book: a person is moved by what they love.
Later in the same book he puts it in four Latin words: pondus meum amor meus.

My weight is my love. A stone falls down, fire rises up, each toward its place, and love, he says, is the pull that carries a person wherever they go. For Augustine, the trouble is rarely that we love nothing.
It's that our loves are out of order. In another book he calls virtue the right ordering of love. So the change he hoped for wasn't more willpower.
It was loving better things, and loving them in a better order. Day five of a test is a good day to borrow him. By day five, effort alone can wear thin.

teach.h: WHAT YOU LOVE CARRIES THE REST.
teach.b: What you love keeps pulling. If one part of your rule is the song you'd replay, it isn't a luxury. It's the weight, and it may carry the rest.

how: Augustine tells the pear theft in book two of his Confessions, and in City of God he calls virtue the order of love. On a personal rule, a test week can include a short note of the part kept gladly, not only the parts kept.

o: the fifth test day: drop the parts that feel too hard
the fifth test day: notice the part of your rule you love
the fifth test day: grade how strictly you kept the rule

games.q: the pear tree: tap the pairs.
p: not even good; thrown to the pigs

s: Augustine stole the pears because he was hungry
he says the pears weren't even good; he loved the stealing, and the company.
"my weight is my love" comes from Augustine's Confessions
pondus meum amor meus: love is the pull that carries a person where they go.
a good rule runs on willpower, not on what you love
for Augustine, love is what moves a person; the loved part can carry the rest.

games.q: a friend training for a race dreads every run except Saturday's, with her running club. by Augustine's teaching, what's going on?
o: she lacks discipline; love shouldn't decide how you train.
the Saturday run is her weight: what she loves can pull the rest.
she should quit, since she clearly doesn't love running.
games.why: Augustine found that even the pears were really about the friends. love is the pull; the loved part, here the club, can carry the week.

practice: Go back over the five days of your test, slowly, one part of the rule at a time. For each part, ask only this: did I love it, or only do it?
Then say the name of the one you'd miss most, out loud, once, and let your hands rest while it comes back to mind.

wordCard.voice: Test day five: the day you notice which part of your rule you love. Augustine's word for that pull is pondus, weight.

orig.note: Latin, from Augustine's Confessions: my weight is my love.

carryVoice: For the road: loved, the weight that carries the rest of the rule. That's day 1695.
